title: To the moon! Navigating deep context in legacy code with Augment Agent — Forrest Brazeal, Matt Ball

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary: Forrest Brazeal (freelance educator, formerly Google, founder of Freeman & Forrest) and Matt Ball (Solutions Architect at Augment Code) present a workshop on navigating legacy codebases with Augment Agent. Augment Code's key differentiator is its proprietary context engine, built over two years, which extracts relevant knowledge from codebases to provide higher-quality inputs to AI models. The product is an IDE plugin targeting enterprise users, with security features including customer-managed encryption keys and ISO 42001 certification. It offers chat mode for simple Q&A with turn-by-turn control, agent mode for complex tasks, and remote agents that run in background and parallel. Auto mode allows agents to execute commands without human permission. The talk uses the Apollo 11 guidance computer codebase as an extreme legacy code example: a monolithic assembly file developed at MIT in the 1960s, available on GitHub. First demo: using Augment chat to explain the 1202 program alarm during lunar descent. The agent identified it as the executive system running out of available core sets, caused by an external radar left on, with the computer offloading low-priority tasks to continue mission-critical operations. Second demo: code modernization using the P65 full-auto landing routine. The presenters set up simulator.py expecting a descent file with a lunar_descent_guidance class implementing P65, then prompted the agent in auto mode to run simulator.py until it succeeds without modifying simulator.py. The agent autonomously mapped the codebase, found the relevant assembly code, created descent.py implementing the P65 vertical descent guidance algorithm in Python, resolved a Python version issue, and successfully ran the simulator, landing within 0-1 meters. Forrest then outlines a three-step methodology for legacy codebases: (1) use the agent to understand the codebase by asking questions in chat, (2) write tests using a blend of chat mode to predict behavior and agent mode to generate tests, and (3) modernize by converting small portions modularly while applying tests. He notes agents can struggle with ambiguity, such as whether priority level zero is highest or lowest. Audience Q&A confirmed the agent handles dependency checking across large codebases and that the demonstrated approach is effectively test-driven development. Real-world equivalents include Java 8 to Java 17 migrations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker backgrounds
sections.summary: Forrest Brazeal and Matt Ball introduce themselves. Forrest is a partner of Augment Code, not an employee. Matt is a Solutions Architect at Augment with prior experience at Postman and as a software engineer. They outline the session: Augment Agent, the Apollo 11 guidance computer, and live demos.

sections.title: Augment Code features overview
sections.summary: Matt describes Augment's three key pillars: the proprietary context engine built over two years, IDE plugin compatibility for enterprise users, and security features including customer-managed encryption keys and ISO 42001. He explains chat mode for simple Q&A, agent mode for complex tasks, and remote agents for background/parallel execution. Forrest notes remote agents may have been used by fast contest winners in a Tuesday workshop.

sections.title: Apollo 11 guidance computer background
sections.summary: Forrest introduces the Apollo 11 guidance computer (AGC) as the 'fourth astronaut.' It was a monolithic assembly codebase developed at MIT in the 1960s, used to land the lunar module, and is available on GitHub. He calls it the ultimate legacy codebase, noting few developers can read assembly confidently.

sections.title: Demo: Understanding the 1202 program alarm
sections.summary: Forrest demonstrates using Augment chat to ask 'what does the 1202 program alarm do?' The agent reads the codebase, finds the octal value 122, explains the executive system ran out of available core sets, and supplements with web context: an external radar was left on. The computer offloaded low-priority tasks to continue mission-critical operations, enabling the landing. Forrest highlights this took ~30 seconds versus a potentially long manual search.

sections.title: Demo: Code modernization with P65 auto-landing
sections.summary: Forrest explains P65 (full automatic landing) vs P66 (manual override used by Armstrong). He sets up simulator.py expecting a descent file with a lunar_descent_guidance class implementing P65, then prompts the agent in auto mode: 'run simulator.py until it succeeds. Do not change simulator.py.' Matt explains the agent uses codebase knowledge as a starting point, explores with the context engine, identifies the missing file, and begins building an implementation plan.

sections.title: P65 demo completion and legacy code methodology
sections.summary: The agent autonomously created descent.py implementing the P65 vertical descent guidance algorithm in Python, resolved a Python version issue, and ran the simulator successfully, landing within 0-1 meters. Forrest then presents a three-step methodology for legacy codebases: (1) use the agent to understand the codebase by asking questions in chat, (2) write tests using chat mode to predict behavior and agent mode to generate tests, noting agents can struggle with ambiguity like priority level conventions, and (3) modernize by converting small portions modularly while applying tests. Audience Q&A confirmed the agent handles dependency checking across large codebases, the approach is effectively test-driven development, and real-world equivalents include Java 8 to Java 17 migrations. Forrest invites attendees to try Augment Agent for free.
